paras: The whipping of Mat Wilson and Lou Clemmons was a night flogging of two women by "a party of lynchers" at Liberty, Casey County, Kentucky, on a Tuesday night, apparently July 30, 1895. The next day the county sheriff jailed the two women at Stanford, and the only report of the whipping, a local correspondence, used it to argue for stricter enforcement of the law rather than lynching.

On the Tuesday morning, two Black men, Neely Northcutt and Isaac Squires of Adair County, had a "shooting scrape in the colored part of Liberty." Brought before Judge Tilford, Northcutt was fined $50 and given 50 days in jail, while Squires was acquitted of the shooting but held for carrying concealed weapons. The correspondent wrote that the affray "came up over two noted courtesans," Wilson and Clemmons, and that the women, with Northcutt and other Black men, had for some time been "conducting themselves in a manner to shock decency."

That night a party of men, unnamed and of unstated number, "severely lacerated the naked backs of the two females." On Wednesday Sheriff Adams took both women to Stanford and lodged them in the Lincoln County jail "for offenses heretofore," to be held until Liberty's new jail was finished.
No report of an arrest or prosecution of the men who whipped the women appears in the coverage.

The episode appeared in the Semi-weekly Interior Journal of Stanford on August 6, 1895, as one paragraph in a column of Liberty news. Its writer called the men "dusky sons of Africa" and the women "courtesans," and granted that "emergencies may arise" justifying a community to "rise in their might," provided those acting were "qualified to cast stones." Yet the same writer judged it "doubtful whether lynching ever does bear good fruit," traced the trouble to "a loose or non enforcement of the laws," and urged a statute and county work-farms.
No other report of the whipping, in either the white or the Black press, appears in the coverage from August and September 1895.

accounts.label: Liberty correspondent
accounts.gist: A night party of lynchers flogged two women whose conduct the writer condemned; the sheriff then jailed the women for earlier offenses. The writer half-excused the community but doubted lynching's value.
